extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, litigators, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on measuring and proving patent damages (lost profits, reasonable royalty, enhanced damages, marking/notice, and willfulness) in litigation, including doctrinal tests and evidentiary rules. Focused on practical standards courts use to evaluate entitlement and amounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of demand / significant sales
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming that the patent owner and the infringer sell substantially the same product, proof of a significant number of sales by the patent owner or the infringer is deemed compelling evidence of demand, the first of the Panduit elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starting point for any lost profits analysis; cited cases include BIC Leisure Prods. v. Windsurfing Int’l and Gyromat Corp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit element: absence of acceptable noninfringing substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent owner must show either that (1) the purchasers in the marketplace generally were willing to buy the patented product for its advantages, or (2) the specific purchasers of the infringing product purchased on that basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Available noninfringing substitutes of significantly higher cost are not acceptable substitutes. Proof may be extrapolated from long-felt need, market surveys showing purchasers would have bought the patentee’s device, or third-party testimony that they would have bought from the patentee absent infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit element: adequate manufacturing and marketing capability
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent owner must prove possession of adequate manufacturing and marketing capability to meet the additional demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If adequate capacity did not exist during infringement, proof of ability to expand suffices. Even if patentee bid on contracts covering only a small portion of infringer’s sales, patentee can recover lost profits on all infringing sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit element: quantum of profit (marginal profit) to be recovered
rubrics_metrics.description: Where diversion of sales is proven, lost profits are measured by multiplying the marginal profit lost on the diverted sales by the sales total that the patent owner would have garnered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gross sales may be proven from infringer’s business records or other reliable sources; uncertainties due to poor records are resolved in favor of the patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: State Industries market-share method
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative analysis approved in State Industries allows the patent owner to assert that but for the infringement it would have sold additional units in proportion to its established market share.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method is not mandatory and applies only if the patent owner and infringer compete in the same market—i.e., infringer’s customers would transfer demand to patentee if infringer’s product were unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire market value rule (1995 Federal Circuit modification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Federal Circuit’s 1995 modification, the entire marginal profit, rather than only a portion, is used to compute damages if the unpatented components 'function together with the patented component in some manner so as to produce a desired end product or result.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies when the patented feature is only a portion of the product but contributes to a combined desired result; cited Rite-Hite en banc decision and accompanying cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marginal profit calculation / incremental cost method
rubrics_metrics.description: Margin of profit is determined by subtracting from expected revenue the incremental or marginal costs the patent holder would have incurred as a result of the increased sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only a reasonable approximation must be proven; uncertainties resolved against infringer. Incremental costs normally include variable costs (direct labor and materials) and exclude fixed costs (insurance, property taxes, administrative expenses). Patentee’s costs may be proven by historical records or reconstructed by expert testimony; if impossible, infringer’s profits or industry margins may be examined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of preinfringement prices in revenue calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Preinfringement prices are generally used in calculating lost revenue so that the patent owner is not penalized because of price erosion caused by illegal competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Price erosion may be taken into account where appropriate; cited cases include Yale Lock Co., TWM Mfg., and Lam, Inc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of reduced sales growth and other projection methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduced sales growth can be considered in calculating lost sales; other acceptable methods include modeling patentee pricing and sales policies as a rational patent-based monopolist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damage to the market from inferior infringing products also may be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovery for accessories/spare parts (post-Rite-Hite)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to 1995, lost profits on accessories, spare parts, and supplies were recoverable when patent owner could normally anticipate sale of the nonpatented component together with the patented; after Rite-Hite, such profits can only be recovered if there is a functional relationship between the unpatented component and the patented invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rite-Hite restricts accessory/spare part recovery—look for functional relationship evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty: established royalty vs hypothetical negotiation
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable royalty may be based on an established royalty (if one exists) or on a hypothetical royalty reflecting an arm’s-length negotiation at the time infringement began between a willing licensor and licensee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Established royalties are usually best evidence but a single license or post-infringement offer may be insufficient. Patentee bears burden of satisfactory evidence on amount of reasonable royalty; courts have wide discretion in approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of the hypothetical licensing negotiation
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothetical licensing negotiation is conducted as of the time the infringement began.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This timing governs projections of anticipated profits, costs, and bargaining positions to be used in the hypothetical negotiation framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia-Pacific factor 1: royalties received for licensing the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Royalties received for licensing the patent in suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as evidence of what is a 'reasonable' royalty where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia-Pacific factor 2: royalty rates for comparable technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Royalty rates for comparable technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparable license rates can guide reasonable royalty determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia-Pacific factor 3: nature and scope of the license
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature and scope of the license (e.g., exclusive versus non-exclusive or territorial restrictions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: License terms affect valuation in the hypothetical negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia-Pacific factor 4: patentee’s policy and marketing practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentee’s policy and marketing practice of maintaining its patent monopoly by refusing to grant licenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refusal to license can affect the reasonable royalty analysis and bargaining positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia-Pacific factor 5: commercial relationship between patentee and infringer
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial relationship between the patentee and the infringer (e.g., whether they are competitors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitive relationship impacts bargaining leverage in the hypothetical negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia-Pacific factor 6: value as a generator of derivative/convoyed sales
rubrics_metrics.description: Value of the invention as a generator of derivative or convoyed sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider anticipated collateral sales of noninfringing product lines when assessing bargaining positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia-Pacific factor 7: duration of the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Duration of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remaining term affects the value of a license and thus the royalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia-Pacific factor 8: established profitability/commercial success
rubrics_metrics.description: Established profitability of the product made under the patent, its commercial success, and its current popularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial success is probative of value and reasonable royalty rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia-Pacific factor 9: advantages of the patented invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Advantages of the patented invention over modes or devices previously used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technological advantages justify higher royalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia-Pacific factor 10: nature of the invention and benefits to users
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature of the invention and benefits to users of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: User benefits speak to the invention’s commercial value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia-Pacific factor 11: extent of infringer’s use
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which the infringer has made use of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greater use by infringer supports larger reasonable royalty award.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia-Pacific factor 12: percentage of profit/selling price normally allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: The percentage of the profit or selling price normally allowed for use of the invention or analogous inventions in the particular business or in comparable businesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry norms for percentages can inform the royalty computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia-Pacific factor 13: portion of profit credited to the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Portion of the profit credited to the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apportionment between patented and nonpatented features is key to avoid overaward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Georgia-Pacific factor 14: expert testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert economic/technical testimony often used to quantify reasonable royalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of settlement royalties and post-infringement offers
rubrics_metrics.description: A royalty paid to settle an infringement claim may not prove an established royalty rate and offers to license made after infringement began do not demonstrate an established rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 408 issues may limit admissibility; courts may increase an established rate to adequately compensate the patentee where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of acceptable alternatives affects royalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Availability to the infringer of acceptable alternatives to the patented device may decrease the royalty rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infringer’s election to infringe and withdrawal from the business after an injunction are evidence regarding existence or absence of noninfringing alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed awards: splitting between lost profits and reasonable royalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixed awards using lost profits for the infringing sales the patentee proved it could have made and a reasonable royalty on the remainder are permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used where patentee could have sold to some but not all of infringer’s customers, would penetrate some but not all geographic areas, or where reasonable royalty exceeds lost profits in some years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking or actual notice requirement under 35 U.S.C. §287(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner seeking damages for infringement that occurred prior to filing suit must plead and prove compliance with the marking or actual notice requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 287(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages may be recovered from when compliant marking began or when actual notice was given, whichever came first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifics of marking requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Marking requires fixing on the patented article the word 'patent' (or 'pat.') together with the patent’s number or, when that cannot be done, a label on the article or package containing like notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to give public notice; marking must be substantially consistent and continuous; limited de minimis exception may exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual notice definition for §287(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual notice sufficient to satisfy §287(a) 'requires the affirmative communication of a specific charge of infringement by a specific accused product or device.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether actual notice was given is determined by patent owner’s actions, not infringer’s knowledge; examples include offers to license, verbal notice with a copy of the patent, or third-party notification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increased damages under 35 U.S.C. §284 (treble)
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages may be increased up to three times at the discretion of the district court under 35 U.S.C. § 284; increased damages are punitive rather than compensatory and serve as deterrent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical context given; trebling discretionary in modern law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure and standard for awarding increased damages
rubrics_metrics.description: District court must (1) find clear and convincing evidence that the infringement was willful (or other circumstances justify enhancement) and (2) determine from the totality of the circumstances that damages should be increased; the court should explain the basis for increasing damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-step test derived from Federal Circuit precedent (State Indus. two-step).

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus of willful infringement inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The infringer’s intent and reasonable beliefs are the primary focus of a willful infringement inquiry; when a potential infringer has actual notice, he or she has a duty to diligently ascertain whether they are infringing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Willfulness relates to culpable conduct—intentional, deliberate infringement—and supports punitive enhanced damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of opinion of counsel in willfulness determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeking and obtaining competent legal advice before initiating possibly infringing activity is commonly cited as an important factor; however, an opinion letter will not necessarily preclude a finding of willfulness nor does lack of one mandate willfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because willfulness arises only if counsel was wrong, the focus is on whether the opinion was sufficient to instill a reasonable belief that the patent might be invalid, not infringed, or unenforceable. Relevant facts include when advice was sought, counsel’s independence, competence, and the extent of analysis performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competency requirements for opinion letters (Underwater Devices standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: An opinion may be competent only if it 'contained within its four corners a patent validity analysis, properly and explicitly predicated on a review of the file histories of the patents at issue, and an infringement analysis that, inter alia, compared and contrasted the potentially infringing method or apparatus with the patented inventions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors bearing on competency include whether counsel examined the file history, whether the opinion was oral or written, in-house or outside counsel, whether from a patent attorney, and whether detailed or merely conclusory. A competent opinion may be irrelevant if the infringer did not rely on counsel’s advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other factors relevant to willfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Other factors include evidence of copying versus attempts to design around the patent and evidence of frivolous litigation defenses versus substantial challenges to the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider these factors among the totality of circumstances in deciding willfulness and whether to enhance damages.
